difficultyRationale: Tests whether the trade-off behind OCP is understood, not just the slogan, by presenting several plausible but mechanical misreadings.
prompt: A junior engineer summarizes the Open/Closed Principle as 'never edit existing classes, always add new ones.' Which statement best corrects this understanding of OCP's actual trade-off?
explanation: Applied well, OCP is a bet on which variations are worth an abstraction; made everywhere, that bet becomes speculative generality that costs more than the if-statement it replaced. The principle is about choosing extension points deliberately, not about a rule against ever modifying a class.

options.text: OCP asks you to identify the axes of variation likely to recur and expose an extension point (an interface or abstract method) for exactly those; it does not forbid ever touching a class, and guessing extension points that never get used adds speculative complexity without benefit.
options.explanation: Correct. OCP is a design judgment about anticipated change, not an absolute rule — an extension point built for a variation that never materializes is pure cost with no benefit.

options.text: OCP means every class must implement at least one interface, since interfaces are what make a class 'closed.'
options.explanation: Implementing an interface does not by itself make a class closed to modification in any meaningful sense, and plenty of classes with no interface at all are perfectly stable; OCP is about where change is anticipated, not about a blanket interface requirement.

options.text: OCP means a class is correct once it compiles without being edited again, regardless of whether new requirements can be met by extension, so a class nobody has touched in years is automatically a better example of OCP than one that gained a single new extension point last month to support a genuinely new, recurring requirement.
options.explanation: Never being edited again could just as easily mean the code is dead or the requirement never changed, not that it was designed for extension; OCP is demonstrated by successfully adding new behavior through extension, not merely by an absence of edits.

options.text: OCP requires every method to be `protected` instead of `private`, so subclasses can override any behavior.
options.explanation: Blanket `protected` access invites subclasses to depend on internal details that were never meant as an extension point, which tends to produce the opposite of OCP's goal: a brittle hierarchy where changing the base class risks breaking subclasses that reached into its internals.
